item.title: リスボンでの学会とマドリードでのPhD Summer School
item.description:
初の学会発表

6月末から7月にかけてポルトガルのリスボンで1週間開催された World Congress of Environmental and Resource Economists (WCERE) で共著論文を発表してきた。これは4年に毎に開催される世界大会で、1700人くらいが参加していたらしい。ヨーロッパの研究機関に所属している人が大半で、米国からは若手の著名な研究者も参加していたが、超大御所の参加はほぼなかったように思われる。

自分はこれまでちゃんとした学会で発表したことがなかったので、このかなりデカい学会が初で最初緊張していたが、知り合いとも話せたり、同僚が彼らの共著者を紹介してくれたりして、充実した初学会になった。

日本人の人も数名見かけて、何名かとは話すこともできた。ただ、アジア人の参加者の中でも中国人とインド人はかなり多く、日本人はギリ二桁いるくらいという感じだったと思う。

会場の Nova School of Business and Economics は民間の資金がかなり投入されている大学らしく、施設の充実度は高かった。キャンパスから徒歩3分でビーチにも着く。学会で提供される食事の質もサービスもかなり高く、場所とサービスの意味でこれ以上豪華な学会は少なくともヨーロッパでは開催できないのでは、と思わされた。

数量空間モデルの Summer School

ヨーロッパのいくつかの大学は毎年夏に Summer School を開催している（お金儲けのためとよく聞く）。代表的なのが PSE, BSE, CEMFI のプログラム。1

1 ある大学では、外部の大学から先生を呼ばず、すべて自分の学部の先生が教えていて、教員が追加の収入を得る場になっているとか……。あくまで人づてに聞いた話だが。

私はマドリードの CEMFI が開催していた数量空間モデル (Quantitative Spatial Models, QSM) の Summer School に参加してきた。内容については検索したらすぐ出てくるので割愛するが、クラスメイトと一緒にご飯を食べたり飲みに行ったりもし、同じ都市・空間経済学や環境経済学に関心を持っている人とも知り合うことができ、非常に有意義な時間を過ごすことができた。講義の内容はまあまあ高度で、私の理解度は半分くらいだったが、今後の研究に活かせる知識を得ることができた。

QSMはざっくり言えば貿易・都市・空間経済学で発展してきた構造推定。過去15年くらいで大きく発展した手法・分野であり、現在研究を取り巻く環境的にも、今後発達してくことは間違いないと思われる。

PhD学生の研究費・お金事情

これらのイベントに参加するためにはそこそこのお金がかかる。今回は両方の参加で日本円では40-50万円くらい掛かっている。これらは全て自分の研究費、学部の研究費と指導教官の研究費から負担して貰っている。（週末も現地に残り遊ぶのに必要な費用は当然自費だが。）

ヨーロッパの大学と言えば主語がデカすぎるし、国によっても国の中でもかなり差があるとは思うが、知っている限り、こちらの多くの大学では日本の大学よりもこれらのサポートも充実しているように思われるので、今後PhD進学・留学を考えている人は、これらの差も考慮してみるのもいいかもしれない。

PhDの給料などの経済状況についてはまた別途記事を書きたい。

item.title: Reflections on 2025 and Resolutions for 2026
item.description:
Reflections on 2025

In 2025, I completed my first-year coursework. In Switzerland (except for the University of Zurich), these first-year courses take place in Gerzensee (I hope to write a separate post about this experience later). To be honest, it was grueling in some ways.

In September, I started my second year as a PhD student. I served as the sole TA for a master’s course, where I gave four lectures on causal inference and empirical project management, followed by supervising student projects. It was a rewarding experience, and I learned a great deal. However, I also realized that I hold very high standards for project management—not only in research but also in general workflows, such as collaborating and coordinating with instructors. I want to improve the course management and organization next year.

Additionally, in November and December, I submitted proposals to two calls for projects, and presented my work at our brown bag seminar.

Throughout the year (especially from September to December), I gained a better understanding of my weaknesses, both as a researcher and as a person—although I have always been aware of most of them. As a non-European PhD student abroad, I have often felt inadequate regarding my abilities, performance, and output. However, I am pursuing my PhD abroad precisely to grow. I need to embrace these weaknesses and work on overcoming them.

Resolutions for 2026

Progress Tracking

  • Review this post monthly to track my progress
  • Manage and monitor my progress

Research

  • Submit our current working paper
  • Present at a conference or workshop at least twice (one is already scheduled for late January)
  • Start a project on bound estimation (an application that can serve as a dissertation chapter)
  • Manage RA time and workload more effectively (ensure clearer communication)

Personal/Career

  • Improve time management (especially for research)
  • Go to bed by 11 pm and wake up at 5 am every day
  • Go running twice a week
  • Achieve a sub-4 hour finish at the full marathon in May

Other Outputs

  • Write at least 10 blog posts (covering research, life, career, and other topics; roughly once a month)
  • Publish 2–3 technical posts on my website

item.title: One economist’s wisdom
item.description:
Lately, my motivation hasn’t been particularly high. A mix of ongoing issues and various annoying commitments has been wearing me down. And, unfortunately, I don’t really have anyone in this city I can talk to spontaneously, either (my spouse is currently in Japan). That said, I’m still working on my R&R with my coauthors and continuing to study a theoretical (econometric) topic I’m currently into.

Every time I hit a low point, and I remember this article, I go back and read it. It always gives me a lift. The paragraph below is from Rubinstein (2013), a rather unusual and personal article where he responds to ten questions aimed at helping “lost” graduate students in economics. I find this particular answer both grounding and moving. It’s one of those things I come back to when I need to remind myself what a rare opportunity I’ve been given, and how how fortunate I am to have it.

Q10. Finally, do you have anything serious to say?

Sure, everything I have said here is very serious. But let me add a final comment: Remember that you are one of the most privileged people on earth. Society has given you a wonderful opportunity. You are supposed to do whatever you want, to think about new ideas, to express your views freely, to do things in the way that you choose, and on top of that you will be rewarded nicely for doing so. These privileges should not be taken for granted. We are extremely lucky, and we owe something in return.

Ariel Rubinstein is an Israeli economist.

Given the current circumstances, and the fact that I have an Israeli friend here, it’s hard not to feel heartache when I think about what many people are going through right now.

Thanks for reading this far.

Rubinstein, A. (2013). 10 Q&A: Experienced Advice for “Lost” Graduate Students in Economics. The Journal of Economic Education, 44(3), 193–196. https://doi.org/10.1080/00220485.2013.795448

item.title: Nobody cites my paper
item.description:
My friend’s paper, published in 2023, has already been cited over 20 times.

My own paper, published in 2024, has only been cited twice. The literature is quite niche, but if my paper had been published a few years earlier (first submission was in 2021), I’m fairly confident it would have received 5–10 citations or even more by now because the seminal work in this field seems to have emerged around that time.

It took me, yes, a very, very long time.

(And just to note: his paper was published in a more recognized journal than mine.)

item.title: Starting a blog
item.description:
Why write?

I enjoy writing short texts every day.
Until recently, I’ve been using Twitter/X for that. But I wanted a space to write in more complete sentences, without thinking about followers.

And, I don’t want to post on my personal website. There are people who view blogging with skepticism, and since I’m in a position where visibility can shape evaluations and outcomes, I’d rather not draw unnecessary attention.

What to expect

Topics will likely orbit around:

  • What everyday life feels like as a foreigner, non-European, a PhD student, and an imposter
  • Empirical work in environmental and development economics
  • Spatial and remote sensing data (analysis)
  • Efficient/reproducible project management (e.g., Git(Hub), {renv}, {targets}) that I enjoy
  • Notes or summaries from articles I read (kind of like TILs)

What not to expect

If you find something useful here, great.
If not, that’s fine too.
